utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll begin today by giving the Trial Chamber's oral ruling on the Prosecution motion under Rule 93 bis to vary the number of witnesses and the length of time available to present evidence. On the 10th of April, 2002, the Trial Chamber ordered that the Prosecution should finish its case within one year of that date, that is, 14 months from the commencement of the trial. The Trial Chamber expressed the view that no trial should last longer than that. On the 25th of the same month, the Appeals Chamber rejected the Prosecution's application for leave to file an interlocutory appeal against the order, finding no error in the Trial Chamber's exercise of discretion or prejudice to the Prosecution, but noting that a Trial Chamber may always reconsider its decision. At the Pre-Trial Conference for the Croatia and Bosnia part of the case on the 25th of July last year, the Trial Chamber, under Rule 73 bis (C) set the number of Prosecution witnesses at a total of 177, and under Rule 73 bis (E), the time available to the Prosecution for presenting evidence as until the 16th of May of this year. The Trial Chamber said that if circumstances altered during the trial, the Prosecution might apply for variation of the order, such variation only to be made for good cause. The Prosecution complains that the original order created what they call an anomaly by setting the number of witnesses and fixing a time available. No anomaly was created. The order was perfectly plain. A hundred and seventy-seven witnesses might be called, and the time available was until 16th of May, 2003. Additional days have been added to the time available, brought about by the ill health of the accused. On the 2nd of April this year, this was announced to be an additional 54 days, which it is now calculated would result in a finishing date of the 5th of September of this year. As of 16th of May, the Prosecution has called 179 witnesses, including 55 in the Bosnia and Croatia part. There have been 192 days of hearing, 95 in the Bosnia and Croatia part. The Prosecution now applies for an order varying that of the 25th of July to allow its case to continue until the Trial Chamber has heard the evidence of all its witnesses in a schedule to its motion or the witnesses whom the Trial Chamber decides should be heard. Moreover, the Trial Chamber should dispense with any fixed date by which the Prosecution case must be concluded. There are now some 118 witnesses left on the schedule I've just referred to, estimated to take about 119 days. The Prosecution also ask for a period to call Rule 92 bis witnesses and estimates it could finish its case in January or February next year. The ground on which the Prosecution seeks this variation is that it is in the interests of justice, under Rule 73 bis (F), to do so in the circumstances which have become clearer as the trial has progressed. Thus while the Trial Chamber could only make a projection in April 2002, now in a better position to make the assessment. The Prosecution claims it has made every effort to meet the timetable and it cannot resolve the time difficulties without being obliged to abandon significant portions of its core case. The Prosecution also applies to the Chamber to vary the number of witnesses and says that it will continue to substitute new witnesses if such become available. The amici submit that the motion should be denied since, if granted, it would make the Prosecution case excessively long and oppressive to an accused having to cope with this scale of trial. They also assert that the amount of evidence and exhibits would become unmanageable. They submit that the Prosecution has not showed good cause for variation so late in the trial, having had sufficient notice of the Trial Chamber's view of the time given, and further submit that it would be wrong for the Trial Chamber to indicate which witnesses should be heard since this would involve the Trial Chamber in the Prosecution of the accused. The Prosecution should be ordered to supply a final list of witnesses in order to enable the accused to have adequate time for preparation of his defence. The background to the application is Article 21 of the Statute, which provides that the Trial Chamber shall ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence with full respect for the rights of the accused. This, of course, means a trial that is fair to both Prosecution and Defence and expeditious for both. However, the Trial Chamber has a wider public duty to ensure that a trial is expeditious and does not consume too much in the way of international time and resources. Against this background, Rule 73 bis (F) provides that during the trial, the Trial Chamber may grant the Prosecution's request for additional time to present evidence if this is in the interests of justice. Therefore, in the present case, the Trial Chamber must be satisfied that it is in the interest of justice to vary its original order of the 25th of July. Put another way, has the Prosecution shown any good cause for the Trial Chamber to vary its original order? Alternatively, have the circumstances altered in such a way that the order should be varied? It is not possible to say, as the Prosecution submits, that the Trial Chamber was not fully informed when it made its original decision. At the time, the trial had been under way for five months. The Prosecution could not complain if there were no extension of time, since it has known for more than a year there would be a time limit and what it was. On the other hand, the Trial Chamber must consider whether it is in the interests of justice so to limit the Prosecution case that it is not able to call as many witnesses as possible relating to its core case. The Trial Chamber has come to the conclusion that it would be in the interests of justice to allow some variation in the time limit to allow the Prosecution more time to call further witnesses it regards as essential. However, the Trial Chamber is also of the view that if granted in full, the Prosecution case would become excessively long and oppressive to all concerned, in particular the accused who has to meet this case and mount a defence. Therefore, a balance has to be struck in the interests of justice. In doing so, the Trial Chamber considers in the circumstances of this case that it would be more convenient to express the variation in terms of hearing days rather than to set a time limit as in the original order. Accordingly, the order of the 25th of July will be varied to allow the Prosecution 100 days from the 16th of May this year as the time available for presenting its evidence. There will be no variation in the order concerning the number of witnesses, but the Trial Chamber has in mind that the Prosecution has not yet identified all its witnesses and that without such a list, it is difficult for the accused adequately to prepare his defence. The Prosecution has indicated that it will finalise the list shortly. The Trial Chamber will keep this matter under review. I deal with one other matter. We have an application in respect of Witness B-024. We grant the protective measures sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are grateful. Your Honour, we are grateful. Before the witness comes in, one other administrative matter, in fact possibly two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One matter. The Chamber may remember that the question of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very sorry. The question of Croatian statehood was something we were going to deal with by a paper that we would serve on the parties and in particular upon Mr. McCormack in his role as the amicus dealing with such matters. We are proposing to do that, I hope, this week. And the particular reason for doing that is then it will be a paper available in advance of the constitutional expert giving his evidence. So -- unless the Chamber has changed its mind on the utility of having such a paper served, given the arrival of Mr. McCormack, that's what we'll do this week. Can I deal with the second matter in just private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And perhaps we could have the witness, please. While waiting for the witness -- he's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us sometime about the programme tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness who comes tomorrow is a witness who must really start -- the witness coming tomorrow is a witness who really has to be dealt with in the day, and it would be convenient if any other evidence can, in the terminology, wrap around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be that this witness's evidence is not concluded, but he'll be able to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, I'm sorry you've been kept waiting. We had to deal with some administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were, as the Court will recall, in the sector of the witness's report headed "Media at the heart of the Yugoslav war," and we had reached pages 59 and thereabouts, but we now come to page 62 of the report, but more materially we come to footnote 138 and clip 11. If that can be played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I have golden teeth in my hand. They told me that these teeth were pulled out with knives from live people who were later killed. "Do you have any examples of somebody being killed or slaughtered or any examples of misdeeds? "I left earlier, but as far as I know, there were other kinds of torture. "What happened? "Well, slaughtering, gouging out eyes, cutting off children's fingers. In baking pans on liberated territories we found children they wanted to roast. Soldiers with heads cut off, the injured were disembowelled, the TO members. So they have no mercy even for the wounded. They have no mercy for anyone. I don't know how that is, they are animals or what, they are not human."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... television output on the 17th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, would you allow me to make two comments before commenting on that excerpt? Thank you very much. If it's possible, I would like us to refer systematically to the fact that the French and English pagination is not the same and I would ask that the paragraph numbers be referred to, because otherwise I find it difficult to find my way around in the text. And in addition, I had some trouble -- that is, I would need some more time in order to find myself, and that's why I'm asking you systematically to indicate the paragraph number so that I can find my way around quickly and not take so much time. Moreover, I wanted to make a comment, rather a clarification about the question I was asked yesterday by Judge Robinson and in respect of which perhaps I wasn't very clear in the answer I gave. Reference was made to the excerpt, the video clip about the excavations and the funeral service that we heard about and the amalgamation that was made between what happened in the Second World War and the situation that reigned in Croatia in the 1990s and 1980s. If I've understood your question, you wanted to ask whether we could talk about lawful or unlawful propaganda before the beginning of the war. If I seemed to you that I was hesitating, it is because that goes back to the question about the legal guards or safeguards that are around it, but I'm not a legal specialist, but it seems very closely connected to me to propaganda, and with your authorisation, I would like to answer about -- your question by adding several things. First of all, there are international texts which prohibit all hateful ethnic or religious hatred. I'm thinking about the International Covenant, Article 20 on human rights, which was ratified by Yugoslavia. And I'm also thinking about the republican federal texts which exist in Yugoslavia. And so as of that time with -- through this type of ceremony, one stigmatises a community - in this case the Croatian Community - as a whole. One could speak about unlawful propaganda whether or not one is in a war context. This is what I wanted to say. And additionally, you also asked me yesterday -- I was a bit nervous, I didn't really mention something. This type of ceremony began as early as 1987 in Serbia and were transmitted on television. And here I can refer you to the work of a French sociologist who is well known, Veronique Nahoum-Grappe, and I refer to this in note -- footnote 93 of the report. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. de la Brosse, and it's entirely my error that I haven't been using paragraph numbers as well as footnote numbers. I will make sure that I do. Reminding yourself of the clip we saw of the teeth allegedly taken out and of the reference to children's fingers, baking pans, and disembowelment, what would be your comment on that clip and its location in your views on propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would note right away is that, speaking professionally, the report is unsatisfactory because the testimony of civilians that was taken -- well, in respect of these alleged atrocities provide no proof for the allegations. And the witnesses are never direct witnesses, eyewitnesses. My commentary is that through this procedure, through an overall judgement depicting the Croats as being inhuman, I think that that appears in the clip. It allows a better justification of the -- of their destruction and their elimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we go now to paragraph 64. It's on page 64 in the English, but it's paragraph 64 as well. May we lay on the overhead projector first of all something from tab 60. This is a part of your report dealing with the way that the Croats were singled out as Ustasha, and it's within a sector of your report headed "Stigmatising the opponent." We see here a report of the 25th of September, 1991, order by the regional territorial Staff Commander saying, item 1: "I order that all enemy's armed forces are called by what is their right and only name, Ustashas." Next, please, tab 61, page 7. This is within an army bulletin document of the 14th of November of 1991. So it's an army document promulgated to army people generally, I think, and it says this: "The liberation of Vukovar, Borovo and Borovo Naselje will bring back freedom to the beleaguered civilian population and above all the Serbs kept there as hostages. Yesterday some 60 persons were rescued from Vukovar. They had survived all the Ustasha horrors, having spent many days and weeks in cellars without enough food or water. They were taken to Vojvodina and are recovering there." Thank you very much. And then tab 63, please. The page numbered 2 at the top. Again from an army bulletin, number 35 of those bulletins, and the date is the 5th of October, 1991. But here we see a statement by the Federal Secretary for National Defence, General Kadijevic. The highlighted passage reads: "Despite our efforts, the events have taken quite a different turn primarily because of the activities of internal destructive forces, but also because of a significant influence of some foreign factors which are deeply involved in everything that is taking place ..." Over to page 3, we see how he characterises what he is describing. Top of the page, please. "In one part of the country, we are being labelled occupiers. The fascist regime in Croatia..." Further down the page: "Acting upon the decision of the SFRY Presidency, our exclusive goal was to prevent bloody inter-ethnic clashes and the repetition of the genocide against the Serbian people ..." Next passage: "What is in force in the Republic of Croatia is neo-Nazism. At present, neo-Nazism is the most serious threat to the Serbian people in Croatia, but it is also diametrically opposed to the vital interests of the Croatian people and any other people in the Yugoslav environment." And finally on this topic, tab 65. This is an order from Colonel Cedomir Bulat dated the 20th of November of 1991 from Tactical Group 2. The highlighted passage of this order, headed "Information On The Goals Of The War" reads: "In these times, the fate our peoples is being decided and we must not allow others to determine it, to destroy us and enslave us." After a gap: "... in this war we defend the right to life and survival, dignity, honour and the right of those peoples of our country who champion the continuation of the mutual living in Yugoslavia." The next paragraph we see reference to the support of Austrian neo-Nazism, the paragraph ending: "... the Yugoslav People's Army had no other choice but to take the war that had been imposed on it and to meet force with force. "JNA is leading a defensive war with very clear goals." A reference to: "Prevention of repeated genocide against Serbs in critical areas." And over the page, please, Usher. "Use this information when preparing for the execution of the coming tasks, in order to make all members of the unit entirely understand these precise goals of the war, adopting them permanently as a main motive for courageous and self-sacrificing conduct in armed combat." Thank you very much. The general topic was singling out Croats and soldiers as Ustasha or as fascists fighting on behalf of Germany. Any comment in addition to what these documents themselves reveal that you would like to add, please?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would like to say, one finds the same terminology used in the Serbian media in order to stigmatise the enemy. I had confirmation of this from journalists whom I met. Having said this, these directives were not written but, rather, oral in which they were asked to speak about Croatian combatants as Ustashas or fascists, using that type of terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the same part of your report and indeed at the conclusion of the same paragraph 64, you will find footnote 143, and can we now please play clip number 12 which comes from the 9th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The panic-stricken Tudjman mercenaries and villains calling themselves the guards have barricaded themselves in the centre of Kostajnica, shooting at everything. We also learnt that a horde of butchers from Tudjman's Black Legion is headed towards Banija. The horde of mercenaries and murderers thirsty for Serbian blood barricaded in Kostajnica seem to realise increasingly that they have been written off."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, your comment on that clip, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an example of what I was just speaking about. Through the vocabulary and terminology used, what they're trying to do is stigmatise the enemy. What is striking here also is that reference is made to what happened during the Second World War at the time of the Black Legion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move to the next paragraph of your report, paragraph 65 within the same topic. It's page 65 in the English version. Can we look at tab 66. Right. There is no tab 66. In which case my error, but we'll go to footnote 146, if we may, and play clip number 13 from the 20th of November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It is known that several dozens of children have fallen victim to the Ustasha knives. Bodies of entire families are still being found slaughtered on the very doorsteps of their homes as well as members of the army. This town is a great Serbian martyrdom. For the past months, Vukovar's outskirts have been the outer limits of a huge concentration camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you want to say about this clip? And if you're able to, what your understanding is as to its accuracy or reliability.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here again one sees the practice of historical amalgamation made between the Croatians and fascists of the Second World War and Tudjman's Croatia. The purpose of the comment on television was to stigmatise the enemy, and I refer to you the terminology that's being used, "Ustasha," and the parallel which is drawn between the situation in Vukovar. The fact that the concentration camps are being used and murders of innocent people, that refers us back once again to the Second World War. Implicitly, the comparison is made with the Croatian concentration camps that existed during the Second World War. The key to the reading of what was -- the key to all of this is to read -- read it as -- to present it in a caricature way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On to paragraph 65, page 66 in the English version, tab 147, clip 14, broadcast on the 5th of April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "After negotiations on peace and only five minutes before the Bajram prayers, the army barracks 'Severni logor' was blown up. It was planned by Ustasha and carried out by jihad warriors with a cruelty typical of both. It marked the first time jihad set foot on European soil."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Similar in part, otherwise different from what we've seen. Your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here again one sees the procedure which is designed to stigmatise the enemy, using certain kinds of terminology which I've studied. I thought I could make an overall comment on both examples which I gave in the footnote, if you allow me. Here once again we see the practice of historical amalgamation starting with facts. One takes note of a massacre of 200 or 300 Serbs in a village and this is linked directly to what happened during the Second World War. And so once again, this is another example of historical amalgamation systematically practised in the media coverage which was done of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina as in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can go back to what I thought was tab 66, and I was wrong, and I think that I'd like your comment, please, on this document which is Exhibit 361, tab 2. Can I -- no. I withdraw that. I'll maybe come back to that later, maybe not. So we'll move on then in the report from footnote 167 to the next subsection, which is headed "Conspiracy paranoia," and we come to paragraph 68 of your report, found on pages 67 and then onto 68 in the English version. If we can look, please, at footnote -- beg your pardon. Can we go -- no. Sorry, Your Honour. I shan't be a second. Can we go to page 68 in the English then and -- no. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is right. Let's go back to page 66, footnote 147. This is all part of paragraph 65, and can we play, please, tab 15 from the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The day on the Mostar frontline up to now has been relatively peaceful without significant armed provocations. However, the Ustashas continue to launch occasional attacks but they're obviously too weak to mount an all-out offensive. Namely, according to military sources, commando units continue to infiltrate liberated territory. Especially worrisome are reports of what's happening to the Serbs of Roska Gora and Bogodol where, according to certain military sources, two to three hundred Serbs were savagely massacred and all their property destroyed. The crime resembles those committed by the Ustashas as long ago as 1944."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there anything additional to your previous comments that you would need to make about that particular clip which exemplifies points you've already made?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- that this shows the -- I confused with the page numbers here but I made comments already about both excerpts, both clips, because I mentioned both of them in that same footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go on to paragraph 68 which, as I said, is on page 68 in the English version. Paragraph 68, and it is footnote 156. It's in the section headed Conspiracy -- or subsection headed "Conspiracy paranoia" and we're going to look at a clip dated the 22nd of November, 1991, showing Kadijevic, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "With pronounced impatience, Germany is for a third time attacking our country. It now resorts to modern methods but it also uses the fascist methods from World War II. Germany then made use of the so-called 'fifth column.' Now it is opting for various other methods of special warfare in preparation for economic followed by military action."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your comment on that, please, Mr. de la Brosse.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example of this alleged plot against Serbia. The example is important because it isn't just anybody who is experiencing it but, rather, the Minister of Defence. If I had any comment to make, I would say that it's one example of many, and what I would say is that the specific nature of Serbian propaganda has to do with the extreme diversity and variety of the groups that were being targeted as enemies or as potential threats against the Serbs. To give you an idea of the variety of those targets, I would simply like to list for you some examples. Among those are the Slovenes, the Albanians in Kosovo, the Muslims and Bosnia-Herzegovina Croats, the Macedonian independence seekers, and the independence seekers in Vojvodina, and those people who would be part of this alleged plot, through the examples that I could get my hands on in the print press and on television, radio, you've got the United States, the Vatican, France, Albania, Austria. And among the organisations which also could be part of that plot are the European Community, NATO, then the United Nations, and institutions like the CIA, the KGB, and the French secret services. Other participants in that alleged plot in Serbia would be the independent press, the NGOs. I could mention the Soros Foundation, the Helsinki Committee or the Serbian opposition. So these are examples, among many others, which demonstrate the extent of the targets that are named as plotting against Serbia. And so there is a message here which is simple to understand and which is to constantly repeat under various forms the same message, and the idea is that the Serbian people is threatened from everywhere and that therefore the idea implicitly suggested is that you are all getting together in order to threaten us and we've got to band together to protect ourselves against that threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that same --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that same topic in mind, could we turn to the last line of your paragraph 69, which can be found in the English on page 70, and it's footnote 161, and it is the next tab, tab 17 -- the next clip, clip 17. Thank you very much. It's slightly longer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It is a total war being waged against our nation, a total war. We are exposed to physical genocide and extermination, spiritual and moral genocide by denying our entity as a nation. It is being waged by armies, politicians, the church, the media, by an entire universe united in winning this war against us and us losing it. I believe that the most important thing of all is to do everything in our power to defend the truth. We must tell that world that these are times of shame and lies and that in these times of shame and lies no means are spared to spiritually annihilate an entire nation. In this spiritual genocide against our nation, an entire civilisation is participating through the so-called mass media."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one has to recall the context in respect of this clip. This is a time when the international community had become more firm against Serbia, and at that point one sees the idea coming out that Serbia was the victim of an international plot which was genocidal, and here this idea is transmitted by Mr. Cosic who was an historical figure in Serb nationalism and additionally he was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which gives credit to that idea. This idea of genocide allegedly perpetrated by the international community on the Serbian people can be found also in the example I have mentioned above.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on in your report, please, to paragraph 71, English page 72, footnote 166 where you, in your report, say that a facet or a further facet of the anti-Serbian plot was the notion of a conspiracy purportedly exercised by internal traitors. So clip 18, please, broadcast on the 23rd of September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Calls upon all its members and citizens to fulfil their civil duty, defend their homeland from fascism and prevent the extermination of the Serbs in Croatia. The Serbs have always managed to recognise and eliminate traitors and we believe that they will be able to do it again."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this example, there is another facet of the idea of a plot, that is those internal traitors, fifth columns getting orders from abroad, that is the internal threat which has to be eliminated. And the context is important here because it is one of war, and broadcasting this type of news can be seen as opening the door to the lynching of any opponent of the regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Move to paragraphs 72 and 73 on page, in the English version, 74 under the general heading "Triumph of disinformation." You speak in paragraph 73 of how information contradicting official propaganda was methodically swept aside, and you cite as a flagrant example the shelling of Sarajevo and Dubrovnik by Serbian forces. Can we look at tab 57, please. Now, this is from the publication Monitor on the 29th of January of 1993 under a headline "The truth was written long ago" and the subject being the Montenegrin involvement in fighting on the Dubrovnik front. If we turn to the third page of this translation of the article, please. Here is some highlighted extracts: "In the days to come, Pobjeda daily newspaper would note that 'courageous scouts' of the Veljko Vlahovic Brigade killed four Ustashas in fighting for the village of Dubravka, and while retreating, the Ustashas looted and torched houses in the village. My unit first saw a Pobjeda journalist on the 7th of October, two days after the article had been published in Pobjeda. "On the 14th of October, 1991, we liberated Plat and Kupari." Further on: "They were reporting that fierce resistance by the Ustasha forces near Plat had been crushed." Gap. "And the bodies of foreign mercenaries were found." Gap. "We heard a lot about foreign mercenaries during those 15 days of warfare. The fear of falling into the hands of various Kurds, Germans or Africans was rife among the soldiers. In fact, during those 15 days, we had not encountered a real military formation nor had a single mercenary outsider been captured or killed." Next paragraph begins: "Plat was taken, in effect, without a fight." Within the next paragraph: "Like ants with a clear and precise task, the soldiers split up in search of war booty. Nothing that might be of use escapes attention." Then at the bottom: "Items that can't be carried are utterly destroyed in an appalling manner. Only the bare walls remain." Your comment, please, on this extract in relation to the Dubrovnik campaign.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is yet another example showing the disinformation techniques that were used in order to deceive public opinion about what was happening actually at -- during the operations. What is striking here, interesting here is that this is the testimony of somebody who participated in the operations and who is taking note of the complete disparity between what he experienced and what was being interpreted by the media in respect of what had happened. This is a classic procedure for disinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 58, please, on the same context, or in the same context. Can we look at the top of the page, please, Usher. Make sure that I'm looking at the right document. Yes, this is from Monitor on the 17th of December, 1992: "We shall win the war, the war force that has been upon us." Now, the version on the overhead projector hasn't been highlighted, by my oversight, for which I apologise, but we can pick it up easily enough. In the first paragraph we see, for example, in the second line: "Liberation --" In the first paragraph, on the second line, we see reference to: "Liberation march against the Ustashas, the Kurds, the carpetbagging mercenaries that, as the listeners were informed, fill Konavle and Dubrovnik." And the next paragraph, second line, we see a reference to the public being grievously astonished. "Revenge was sought. Combative ardor flared up, precisely what General Torbica had intended to achieve." And three lines on a reference to the MUP, Ministry of Interior losses of 600 to 700. And the following page at the top paragraph, it gives an example of the flavour of this article. The second line from the top. Thank you very much. "In practice --" Second one, that's fine. "In practice, the disarmament of all the paramilitary formations that the Ustasha government had for a long time been aiming against the territory of Montenegro and Herzegovina was being carried out, the basic objective being to carry the civil wars to those areas too." The next paragraph beginning: "Saying that the leaders of Montenegro had several times warned the Ustasha government ..." Further references to Ustasha in that paragraph. And in the quotations I think from Pavle Strugar in the following paragraph which we can see if you go down a little bit. Four lines up from the bottom of that paragraph. "They exercised Ustasha's good knowledge of their terrain." The next paragraph begins with reference to the Ustasha government. And to save time, if we just turn swiftly over to page 3, cast our eyes down the first fresh paragraph, with this line -- really four lines down: "Marovic picturesquely explained that once the fascists had the Jews and the Ustashas the Serbs, and we believed that history would never be repeated. Unfortunately, said he, life did repeat itself and so did historical tragedy." And then we have explanation for the Dubrovnik operation by Marovic. And the next paragraph, Milo Djukanovic, the Montenegrin Prime Minister, quoted as: "Because we had to talk on the Croatian side with Ustashas, hypocrites, criminals, frenzied bloodsuckers - in a word, mercenaries - whose mission was to break up the state of Yugoslavia." Going on to say they committed genocide. Well, I've perhaps taken enough of the court's time with this particular article. Your comment on it insofar as your previous comment doesn't cover it adequately.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is an example yet again of terminology and the use of certain procedures that we talked about already, so I have no specific comment to give you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we move to footnote 177 at the end of paragraph 74, the same -- the end of paragraph 73, I beg your pardon. The same paragraph, the same general topic. Can we look at footnote 177, which is on page 75 of the English version, and it is clip 19 and it deals with the University of Sarajevo's library fire.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Last night in Sarajevo there was a fire in the university library. Luckily, the invaluable cultural treasure had been moved out of it two months before. It is now difficult to establish what exactly caused the fire. True, there was heavy fighting here Trebevic last night. We scrutinised the facade for shell damage close up but were unable to find any. We noticed, however, that the flames licked from within. It all points to yet another Muslim manipulation like the one in Dubrovnik when car tyres were set on fire, something we've already seen."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your comment on this, Mr. de la Brosse, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would say is that the information, which contradicts the official version of what happened, is either omitted or is distorted in order to make it closer to the official version. So this is an example which refers to -- to an involuntary -- to another manipulation which was mentioned a few minutes ago, that is the shelling of Dubrovnik which was presented to the television viewers in Serbia as something which had been concocted by the foreign cameramen who were simply mixing up -- were burning a tyre in front of the camera so that many people would think that there had been shelling. So this is an example of disinformation and manipulation, one of many examples, that happened in Dubrovnik. There would be others in Sarajevo, and I refer to these in my report. What -- the attempt is being made to shift the responsibility onto somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For those looking at the index to your report, we move from the second part, "Media and the service of war," and its third subsection, "Triumph of disinformation," to part three of your report which, if the index can be laid on the overhead projector, shows - and I'm only going to deal with this in summary to save some time - that part 3 is bringing into line any alternative information or opinion as a condition for official propaganda to succeed. And you have three sections to this part of your report. First, how the Serbian press was under tight surveillance. Second, how war propaganda and national cohesion operated during the Kosovo war. And third, the reasons for the impact of propaganda on public opinion. If we start with the first part of your report, and there are now only, I think, a couple more paper references - three- and one more video to look at, you deal with the tight surveillance of the Serbian press starting at, in the English, page 79 and paragraph 79. You cover the psychological pressure imposed on recalcitrant journalists, the rejection of media broadcasting federal information, and you then turn to a plan of action that you say can be evidenced against an independent press. And if you would be good enough to find yourself at paragraph 83, which in the English version is at page 81, it may be helpful if we look at two documents. One will be tab 22. Looking here, Mr. de la Brosse, at a special decision by the Human Rights Committee concerning reports of particular states, and the date of this document is 1992, I think. And we can see, under the decisions taken, on the first page highlighted -- a little further down, please. Highlighted under -- that under Article 14 of the relevant Covenant: "Measures were taken to combat advocacy of national, racial, or religious hatred constituting incitement to discrimination hostility or violence in relation to Article 20 of the Covenant." That was in respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Over the page, we can see something similar for Croatia. And then at the foot of that page, under heading C, Human Rights Committee expressing its concern. Over the page, please. And acting under the Covenant, took measures to combat advocacy. First of all, it requests the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to submit a report, and then it deals with measures taken to combat advocacy of national, racial, or religious hatred. Your comment, please, on this document.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment and the lesson I can draw from this is that the authorities of the Serbian Montenegrin republic were aware of the harmful influence of certain media in their territory, were transmitting messages of racial or religious nationalistic hatred and hostility, encouraging violence, and under the legislation which was in force, steps were to be taken to make all of this incitement stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You will remember the question of connection that His Honour Judge Robinson asked you yesterday at an early stage. Does your comment on this document connect also to that question?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look, in addition, at an already exhibited document, Exhibit 359, tab 3. And it's pages 23 and 24. Effectively, I think, 23. That document. This is a Human Rights Watch document, and it deals, on the highlighted passage, with press restrictions, saying that: "Helsinki Watch is concerned about reports that the Yugoslav army is forcing local newspapers in Kragujevac and other areas in inner Serbia to print lists of persons who the JNA claims are army deserters who fled from the battlefields in Croatia. Military authorities purportedly intended to post such lists in public areas. At anti-war rallies in Serbia, petitions were signed protesting such action by the Yugoslav military." And later: "Helsinki Watch is concerned that the public disclosure of the names of purported deserters could lead to reprisals against them or their families by paramilitary groups or individual extremists. Moreover, by demanding that local newspapers publish such lists, Yugoslav military authorities are interfering with freedom of the press." Perhaps we can just turn over about -- a few -- yes. Very well. We'll stick with that one quoted passage. This again, does this show the state of knowledge on the basis that the Human Rights Watch report is correct?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment is that at issue here is an additional warning to the authorities in respect of unlawful and dangerous practices. I think that the document is interesting. I don't think I read the whole document, but the passage does show clearly that what is being designated is trying to make public opinion think a certain way, which is not doing what was expected. And the document also makes one think -- I know that one should -- reference made to the statement. I refer to the list of journalists who were deviating or who were not sufficiently -- not sufficiently controlled at the beginning of the 1990s. I'm thinking about a list that was set up by Vojislav Seselj which was read out on television and which called for the elimination of certain recalcitrant German -- journalists. I met some of them in Belgrade. So this is a procedure of revenge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next sub-part of your report on this general topic, which was "Serbia press under tight surveillance," is headed "Direct involvement of the Milosevic couple," and it's paragraph 86, to be found on page 82 of the English version. And if we may see part of tab 4. And it's the second page of this exhibit. If the usher would -- sorry. These are first an extract from Jovic's diary. It's footnote 197 in the paragraph concerned, and it says this in the paragraph of the report: "Milosevic's wife started to publish a series of articles in the Duga magazine in the form of her diary and thoughts in which she touched on numerous political and social issues but also announced what could later happen or what should happen. Everything she announced really did happen. What she objected to would be publicly attacked." Then later, he says: "A phantom which could destroy one single sentence hovered above the people."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next highlighted passage -- yes. Can we play this? We've now found the French clip, Your Honour. Can we play the last clip? And I think that Your Honours do have a transcript of it. Clip 20.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That's how it worked. What you saw on the state channel, the war mongering discourse and practices, that we're now able to lay bare. The false information and fabricated reports. Milosevic gave his orders directly to the director of the television station."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That, I think, was Dusan Mitevic, formerly a director of the RTS speaking. Your comment on these two exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm having a problem with the interpretation. I don't catch all the names. I heard -- didn't hear Mitevic, I think it should be Mitevic. This clip omits the fact that false information is being practised, and it refers to fabricated reports. And in the interpretation that I heard, that's what I heard, but I don't know if you got it. It talks about false information and fabricated reports. My comment therefore would be that within those closest to Milosevic, this direct involvement of President Milosevic is supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next section of your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what's the source of this last clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the witness can tell us the source of the last clip. It's an interview in the documentary "Milosevic: A very modern dictator," and it was BBC in association with France 2 and France channel 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. de la Brosse?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the next section, as I've already explained, was "War propaganda and national cohesion during the Kosovo war." It's paragraph 93, Mr. De la Brosse. It's page 85 in the English. And may we look, please, at tab 20. Now, this is a document, so that we can explain, that I think you found or located on a web -- on a website; is that correct? Or somebody else did. And -- tell us, therefore, the website you got it from and when.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the 92 site -- B92 site. It's indicated on the address you have on the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can see that the highlighted passage that I want to be on the overhead projector - thank you very much - is headed "Serbian Information Ministry, instructions for the operation of news agencies and media outlets in the circumstances of imminent war danger." I will read half a dozen of the paragraphs. 1. "Media operators to establish 24-hour monitoring and permanent contact with state agencies." 5. "Reports on losses and casualties of the Yugoslav army and the Serbian police are strictly prohibited." 6. "Every journalist in the field or in the newsroom must be at the service of the state's current interest and participate in the system of reporting and information." 8. "Police and army actions must be described as defence activities or the struggle to preserve and defend the country." 9. "Enemy losses should be described by terms 'neutralised,' 'incapacitated,' 'paralysed' and 'liquidated.'" 10. "No information which would spread defeatism and panic must slip through the hands of the editor-in-chief." 13. "The so-called Kosovo Liberation Army must be referred to as 'a gang,' 'terrorists' and 'criminals.'" 14. "NATO forces must be referred to as the aggressor." 15. "Media operators are required to emphasise that army and police personnel are fighters for the freedom of the country." Well, describe the origin, so far as you're concerned, of this document. First of all, is what's described there consistent with the material that you have been examining, the raw material that you've been examining?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: These instructions come from the Serbian Ministry of Information, so this is at the time where the air war had begun. I'm sorry, I got a comment from the interpreters in French. This is the time when the air war was about to begin or had already begun. It was the 24th of March, 1989. So we have a reading list, in a way, that was imposed on the press. There was absolutely no latitude in respect of information, and information was held back at the source, comments were dictated to the journalists. And so we are dealing with de facto censorship and suppression of any press freedom. It was 1999. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, is the document we are watching through the ELMO or tab 20 the original one or the translation of what is posted on the website?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the internet site there -- you have the version in English and in Serbo-Croat. So I read the English version. It isn't a personal translation that I made or a translation that anybody else made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two more paper references. I see the time. I have located what I misdescribed -- or to be more precise, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff has helped me locate what I misdescribed as tab 66. If I can deal with that. It's, for those looking for it, it's an already tendered exhibit; 361, tab 2. The Chamber and Mr. de la Brosse may wish to return to paragraph 65, which in the English is materially on page 65. And to remind the Chamber and those listening, this is within the subsection headed "Stigmatising the opponent." The document itself, which we can see on the overhead projector is from the publication Narodna Armija from the 9th of January, 1992, the headline "The truth has broken all barriers" and "A soldier's story." He deals -- we needn't trouble with the first page. If we go to the third page, a daily situation analyses where he deals with the complex task he, the author of this account, was given, was complex, he says. And then we see the highlighted passage, "who felt proven hatred." "Of particular concern to us was the enemy who felt proven hatred of JNA members." Further down, highlighted: "The enemy's operations were hard to predict because they used all kinds of tricks and attacked perfidiously." Further on: "I personally realise that it was important in this war, as we were up against an enemy fighting an extremely dirty war. In particular, we made a big effort to explain this to our soldiers, who were eager to fight but were not used to such perfidiousness on the part of the enemy." Next page, the last document we're going to look at. "Proven courage of our soldiers. I also want to point out the selfless courage of our soldiers. They all wanted to fight. They all conducted themselves bravely. However, I want to point out that political intrigue by some parties created considerable confusion amongst our troops." Next passage: "The population was in fact terribly indoctrinated, especially the Muslims and Croats. They were scared by the arrival of Montenegrin and Serbian soldiers so that sometimes we arrived in almost completely evacuated villages while in other villages people received us with fear. After awhile, however, this fear disappeared as they realised that the soldiers had not come as occupiers but as liberators. Later, we had friendly encounters with locals bringing fruit and cakes to our soldiers, treating them to what they had." And finally: "I believe this is one of the greatest achievements. In Dubrovnik they also realised that the JNA had not shelled them despite their fierce propaganda which always pointed that out." Within the context of your subsection "Stigmatising the enemy," your comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the terminology used to characterise the Croats in general, speaking about -- when they use the expression "Ustasha fighters" or "Muslim fighters" as being jihad warriors, this is also found in the description of the combats -- of the combat itself. I go back to page 71 of the report in French. The reports ordinarily showing the Serbian troops show no images of destruction of civilian victims when the Serbian troops attack a town, this is systematically shown as a defence mechanism or shown as the liberation of a town. This was seen in the media coverage of Vukovar and also in respect of what happened in Sarajevo. So here we in some ways are dealing with the promotion of prettified images, showing good Serbs as opposed to a bad enemy, which is stigmatised both through terminology used to describe the enemy and the atrocities which allegedly are committed by that enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask of the witness unless there's anything -- let me just deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. de la Brosse. The balance, of course, of your opinions are as expressed in your report produced as an exhibit to this Court.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that's all I'm going to ask but will just consider it with Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff over the break if the Court is about to have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add one question or topic arising simply from His Honour Judge Robinson's question of yesterday morning when he noted of a report that we'd been considering that the connection was drawn between nationalists' rhetoric and the commission of fearful atrocities, and His Honour observed that the witness would be able to substantiate that connectoral link between national rhetoric and the commission of fearful atrocities, but I forecast that we might deal with it later. I made a reference to that question when dealing with tab 22, I think, earlier this morning. It's right we should take the witness and the Court to paragraph 4 of his report. Lay that on the overhead projector. It's at page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse, page -- paragraph 4 begins with this assertion: "With the media acting as go-between, nationalist political propaganda prepared and conditioned public opinion for the war, so fostering the worst atrocities perpetrated in furtherance of the ethnic policies." Now, that conclusion may be a conclusion apt to be drawn by political scientists or sociologists or others. Can you please help us with how you draw that conclusion yourself.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we are dealing with social sciences, not the natural sciences. It's not always easy to demonstrate the effects that -- that the broadcasting of different messages could have on the public by simply looking at the terminology and the vocabulary which is used in order to describe the adversary. What I would like to say is that I myself relied, or actually I studied the role of the media and tried to show what were the mechanisms used for propaganda being used in the media. The media, after all, are only actors among other actors even if they represent the most convenient way of reaching the largest amounts of people in the population, that is, public opinion. What I wish to add is that through the use of the Serbian resentment against other groups and the designation of scapegoats by the use of vocabulary which is being used in order to denigrate the different groups, so much so that sometimes that group is not given any kind of human qualities, this was able to facilitate the commission of crimes. The vocabulary which was used in the media but not only in the media, this vocabulary was reappropriated by the public, and I was struck by that in the conversations that I had with journalists in Belgrade who explained to me that the public spoke the way people spoke on television, and that one -- that that vocabulary was never neutral. Even if propaganda is a virtual weapon, and in that respect it should be distinguished from what one would call in English "a smoking gun," that propaganda does designate the road which was taken, the behaviour which was adopted, and what the enemy was that had to be eliminated. I would perhaps like to go back to the very definition of propaganda which I give in the report, but I think that it would be important to recall that in this -- before this Court. That propaganda is ordinarily called all of the techniques used to influence people on a political level. And so its objective is to influence the behaviour of the public or have it take on as its own certain ideas. The vocabulary is used in order to transmit that propaganda, and it is a way of allowing my -- in my opinion, that was a way of allowing the consequences of the propaganda to take effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. If I cut you short, please conclude.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add that, for the propaganda to be fully effective, all the more effective insofar as you -- in a specific society in -- would not have the possibility with a video to bring out different opinions. Counter opinions. And it becomes all the more effective if only one truth is distilled for public opinion. That's what I attempted to show or to have understood in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nice, if I have a difficulty with it, it is the categoric, unequivocal way in which it is framed. As he says, we're not in the realm of natural sciences; it's social sciences. If it were framed in some other way not so categoric. For example, "likely to lead to atrocities." But in this categoric manner, I don't know whether it can be substantiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's helpful to know that concern, and Mr. de la Brosse hears you first before I come to the supplementary question I would ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any observation you'd like to make in relation to His Honour's concerns about the categoric nature of your assertion in paragraph 4 or in the report that we read yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I perhaps should have emphasised the fact that these are social sciences that we are dealing with and that things are not always so easy to demonstrate as would be the case in the natural sciences. Having said this, however, the formulation perhaps may be a bit overly-stated, but nonetheless, I reach the same conclusions that Mr. Mazowiecki reached in his report. Perhaps I allowed myself to be influenced, when I drafted this sentence, by the very powerful conclusions that we find in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is my last supplementary question on this topic and the last question I want to ask you is this: Is there anything you feel able to say from all your diverse social science background, anything you feel able to say about what -- what other elements may co-exist - for example, the nature of government or the existence of fighting or whatever - what other elements may exist that make a fertile bed for propaganda to flourish in its effect? Is there anything you want to say about that? It's a long question.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a few minutes ago, the media are only one of the instruments which transmit that propaganda. There are other agents for socialisation which can be used which have an influence on the way that the public views things. Among these others, the other players, the other actors, of course there are the intellectuals, there's the church, there are the politicians. And so we see that within these various groups the themes that we see within the media were also transmitted and so the media are one player among others. The difference is to be found in the fact that they are able to reach the largest numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. de la Brosse. You will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have, we've decided, three and a half hours, if you wish it, to cross-examine this witness. Of course, if you don't want to take that long, that's a matter for you, but we have in mind the length of the Prosecution's examination but also the fact that there is this report on which you are entitled to cross-examine the witness. If you'd like to begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would first of all like to clear up this matter of time, Mr. May. Namely, Mr. Nice said at the beginning that he would go through the report very quickly, focusing mainly on its structure and only rarely would he quote certain passages from it, which means that he endeavoured to shorten his time as much as possible on the understanding that this report, as you see, has a hundred pages plus these two binders which, let it be said in passing, we received only yesterday these two binders, are documents that we are familiar with. So he himself said that he would expedite things and that he would only select a few examples. As far as I'm concerned, in addition to matters of structure and other points made by Mr. Nice, I do have to enter into the very contents of this report. Therefore, I certainly need more time for this witness than the time you have allotted to me, which is more or less the same time given to Mr. Nice. So I expect you to give me a longer period to cross-examine this witness. I think these are arguments that cannot be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, in fact it's not right that it's the same as the Prosecution. We have built in an extra hour for you to examine on the report, but we will review the position at the end of the time. It depends partly what use you make of the time and how expeditiously you deal with things. We will consider it in the light of those matters, but let us begin now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. de la Brosse, tell us begin with the remark made by Mr. Robinson a moment ago and your general response to that question. The critical word -- the critical point is your categorical assessment of certain phenomena. Towards the end of your testimony today, you explained as propaganda or, rather, propaganda as a distorted representation of reality and a series of expressions were used. The implication is that you know the truth and you are comparing what you analysed with the truth. Is that right, Mr. de la Brosse?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that there is an absolute truth. I am claiming that the way that information was dealt with and commented on was not sufficiently varied, that it was a one-way street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will challenge that later, but let me refer to a few things that you characterised as propaganda a moment ago and as distorting the truth. For example, you quoted that, regarding the NATO forces that committed an aggression, it is suggested that the term "aggressor" be used for them. Is it your opinion that they were not an aggressor?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I have to qualify -- characterise NATO as an aggressor. It was an intervention which does not fall within my analysis. The way that I spoke about that event that you are alluding to has to do with the way the media spoke about it. I'm not making any statements on whether or not NATO's intervention was well-founded. That is what you are alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But wasn't a war waged against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is where we waste time, you see, with argument with the witness. The witness is here dealing with propaganda. It's not for him, as he says, to characterise it. It may be a matter which we have to decide at the end. But going over old ground is not going to help us and it's not going to get you more time. So let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned the KLA, that it should be described as a terrorist organisation. Do you believe that the truth, according to you, means that the KLA was not a terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having mentioned the KLA. Could you give me some more information, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a reference -- it's a reference in the document which you produced. May we be reminded of the tab number? I rather think it was one of the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the document is being used as an example of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what if it so happens that this is an example of the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 20, we think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The very recent document that the witness has in mind, the Serbian Ministry of Information document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's item 13 on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. de la Brosse, that is the reference, 13, "The so-called KLA must be referred to as 'a gang of terrorists and criminals.'"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me go back to the approach that I used when I prepared the report. What I tried to do, and I hope that I succeeded, was to -- to take apart the different propaganda mechanisms and show how they worked. I'm not an expert in the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia. And for your version to be correct or for it not to be correct is not the issue here for me. What I'm interested in, as somebody who studies propaganda, was the way the facts are presented and interpreted, either correctly or incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you make your question a little bit clearer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point is that you use this document that you're holding in your hand as an example of propaganda or of a distorted presentation of the truth. And what are we going to do if it so happens that that is in fact the truth? Why should that then be considered something inappropriate for the media to report on? I even believe that it was mildly put to call them terrorists. They should be called drug Mafia, and many other terms could be used to describe the worst kind of crime that was engaging in within the so-called KLA.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we've got to go back to the meaning of or the significance of this and the reading list that was imposed on the journalists, the way that information was dealt with and the latitude that was left to the journalists for dealing with information. It was absolutely zero. They had no latitude. I go back to the context of the time when most of the independent or alternative media were either prohibited or, because of this reading list imposed on them, had to deal with information a certain way only. What I wanted to emphasise was the way that the Serbian public learned about what was going on in Kosovo, that it was a one-way street, a unilateral approach, and in that case we are here confronted with a propaganda procedure. I'm not making any judgements about the truth or the non-truth of whether or not the KLA was a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you have just passed judgement by saying that the media had no freedom, that the journalists had no freedom. Where did you get that idea from, that the journalists had no freedom? Do you know that for a fact? Just tell me, please. You're claiming that. That is what you assert, and then we'll move on. We'll come to those questions later.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided a list of the different methods that were used in order to limit or to silence the journalists by obstructing their freedom of speech. I published these in different categories in a document that was given to you, and that is what I base myself on in order to support this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that reporters didn't have any freedom. Very well. Now, tell me in answer to a few more preliminary questions, why do you believe, for instance, that reports on various atrocities were propaganda? If it so happens that they may be truthful, do you believe that the press should have kept quiet about them? And if they don't keep quiet about them, then it's propaganda. I'm talking about a series of examples that were shown here.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For instance, you had here - one of the most recent examples - of a video clip showing teeth that were extracted and a reference made to mutilations and massacres. What are we going to do, Mr. de la Brosse, if that is truly the truth? As an expert for the media, do you believe that the media should have kept quiet about them if these were atrocities committed against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The example that you are referring to I think it has to do with the passage where you see teeth that allegedly were torn out of Serb mouths, the -- by the Croatian fighters, and the interview of a old man in a uniform. Is that the example that you're using?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I've only taken one example. So my question is a more general one: Why reports about events, about real atrocities are considered by you to be propaganda. As an expert for the media, should this have not been reported at all so as not to disturb the public?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem with the example that you are referring to is that - and that's what I want to emphasise now - is the way that information was produced. It doesn't really -- it's not solid, because at no point is any eyewitness mentioned and absolutely no proof is provided in the report of the fact that this took place or didn't take place. I'm not saying it didn't, but there's no proof that it did. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 20793 to 20800. Do you understand the nuance that I'm trying to put forward here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's asking you questions, but you can make your points. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do indeed understand the difference, but your testimony is also in the service of the demonisation of the Serbs, which has been going on for a whole decade. I do understand the distinction. Let me ask you a few more preliminary questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're not going to put that allegation and get away with it like that. Now, Mr. de la Brosse, what he's put is that your evidence, he puts it, is in the service of the demonisation of the Serbs. Now, you should have the chance to answer a serious allegation like that. Is that what your evidence is in service of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not, Mr. President. I was simply referring to what I said a little while ago in order to characterise the specificity of the Serbian propaganda. That is the idea of paranoia. I referred to a long list of people and organisations, groups who were targeted by that type of practice, and I believe that it fits into this kind of reasoning with the purpose of which would be to discredit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please answer a few more preliminary questions for me and then we'll move on to some others. You mention here a large number of examples, and we also saw some video clips which, for instance, say -- use the term "Muslim extremists did this and that," "The Ustashas," "The Ustasha combatants did this and that," "such-and-such misdeeds," and you claim that when the term "Muslim extremists" is used, the reference is to all Muslims. When the term "Ustasha fighters" is used, that that is used to imply the Croatian people. And neither of these is true. For example, in Kadijevic's statement, the one that you quoted from and showed a video clip of, didn't you hear him talk about all peoples and him saying that when talking about the Croatian people, that the atrocities that were taking place were to the detriment of those same Croatian people? So how can you, in view of the examples you yourself have given, say that when the term "Muslim extremists" is used the reference to all Muslims, and when "Croatian criminals" is used the reference is to all Croats? For example, the events of the 11th of September committed by Muslim extremists, condemnation of that event, is that condemnation of all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your question has lasted two minutes, and how that can be a question, I simply don't know. Let's try and construct a question out of it. Well, I think the point -- just a moment. Since you're not going to ask a question, I'm going to ask it for you. The first point that's made is that the references to "Muslim extremists" and "Ustasha fighters" is not true as an example of a reference to all Muslims and all Croats. So I suppose what is being said is that there are plenty of other examples, including what Kadijevic said, which show people talking in more general terms about the Croatian people and the Muslim people. So I suppose one could put it this way: Is your description of them as extremists or Ustashas, is that an exaggeration of what was in fact broadcast or written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I mean is that the examples that were discussed and shown today and yesterday, these come from the report, and there are several of them. The least thing that I could say with a little bit of distance in respect of the examples that I had access to don't all appear in the report. I mean by this that even if there were sometimes counter examples implicitly, or explicitly in fact, what is shown -- well, how should I say? The -- systematically there is a generalisation made. When it applies to an entire community, an adjective which is extremely pejorative -- the fact that one speaks about, for instance, the Croats as "Ustasha combatants," when you're part of the Serbian public and you know about the historical context of the Second World War, I think that the connection is made in the minds of people, that is, the Ustashas today are the ones who perpetrated yesterday's atrocities and so one must be distrustful of them. There are many, many examples in the report which I can't -- I don't have it immediately in my -- at my fingertips there, I can't give them to you right now. I -- in order to do so, I would prefer to refer you back to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is this, Mr. de la Brosse: How can you use the expression "Muslim extremists" and identify it with all the Croats, for example, or the Ustasha Bojovnik, the Ustasha fighters or combatants, how can you identify that with all the Croats? That's what I wanted to say. And the Muslim extremists, how can you identify that as meaning the whole of the Muslim population? I assume that when you use the word "extremist," it doesn't apply to all the Muslims, or if you say "the Ustasha combatants," it doesn't apply to all the Croats by the same token. So how are you able to draw the conclusion that what is implied is all Croats or all Muslims? How are you able to come by that particular conclusion then?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've got to put the process of the generalisation together and we have to compare that with the fact that, through the media, a certain number of statements by officials were -- political officials were made. Officials from the Serbian government, officials who made the connection much more explicitly. When you hear somebody -- I'm sorry, I really don't pronounce the names very well, the Serbo-Croat names. When you're talking about Mrs. Plavsic, when she said that the Muslims have a genetic heritage which is inferior and degenerate, when you hear statements by a leader who is a Serb leader in Bosanska Krajina, when you hear that person say that children from mixed marriages, he's referring here -- I'm not quoting it exactly, but that those children are -- are -- should be turned into soap, that's all that they're good for, that's a general context which means that the connection and the generalisation, at least from my point of view, the connection is made in the public -- in the public mind. I could also mention statements -- there are many of them in the report, in the footnotes. We could mention somebody like Vojislav Seselj, things that he said about the Croats.
